summary: Discusses security threats to network-based localized mobility management on two interfaces: between a localized mobility anchor and a mobile access gateway, and between the gateway and a mobile node. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo lists the ways an attacker can get at a mobile device's traffic in a network-based mobility system. It covers the link between the central anchor and the local gateway, the link between the gateway and the device, and floods arriving from elsewhere on the Internet.

subtitle: What can go wrong in the two interfaces a network-based mobility system relies on.

tldr.problem: Network-based localized mobility management removes mobility software from the device and puts the work in the network, which creates two new interfaces where an attacker can try to take over a node's traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the threats on the interface between the localized mobility anchor and the mobile access gateway, and on the interface between the gateway and the mobile node: compromising or impersonating either end, man-in-the-middle attacks, IP spoofing, and flooding from the wider Internet.
tldr.outcome: The document names the threats but does not fix them: the mitigations and the security considerations that come with them are left to the protocol specifications for the two interfaces.

It lists threats only: the mitigations and the security considerations that come with them are left to the protocol specifications for the two interfaces. The sibling RFC 4830 sets out the problem the architecture solves.

sections.title: The Architecture and Its Two Interfaces
sections.content:
Network-based localized mobility management, or NETLMM, lets IPv6 mobile nodes move around inside a domain without any mobility support in their network stacks. A node keeps its IP address constant as it moves from link to link, which avoids the signaling overhead and the latency of changing the address. Software specifically for localized mobility management is not needed on the node, though IP-layer movement detection software may be, and link-layer mobility driver software is a prerequisite.

The IP addresses of mobile nodes carry a prefix that routes to a localized mobility anchor (LMA). The anchor holds an individual route for each registered mobile node, and that route terminates at a mobile access gateway (MAG), the gateway the node attaches to on its current access link. The gateway is responsible for updating the node's route on the anchor as the node moves. It detects the node's arrival from handoff signaling that the node pursues, and may also watch connectivity to notice when the node leaves its access link.

That gives the architecture two interfaces: the interface between a gateway and an anchor, where route update signaling occurs, and the interface between the node and its current gateway, where handoff and other link maintenance signaling occur. The architecture demands no specific mechanism for detecting arrival and departure. It may be entirely at the link layer, as is common for cellular networks, in which case the IP layer never detects any movement, even when a node moves from one link to another handled by a different gateway. If the link layer cannot provide the needed function, the node must perform IP-layer movement detection and auto-configuration signaling, which triggers the gateway's route update. A mobile node identity, established by the domain when the node first connects and authenticates, lets the gateway ascribe the decisive link- or IP-layer signaling to the correct node. It is conceptually independent of the node's IP and link-layer addresses, but it must be securely bound to the node's handoff signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: The design keeps a device's IP address the same while it moves and lets the network handle the change. That leaves two places to attack: the link between the anchor and the gateway, and the link between the gateway and the device.

sections.title: Threats on the Anchor-to-Gateway Interface
sections.content:
The protocol on the interface between the anchor and the gateway establishes, updates and tears down the routes that carry mobile nodes' data traffic. Threats to this interface fall into three groups: compromise or impersonation of the anchor, compromise or impersonation of the gateway, and man-in-the-middle attacks.

A compromised anchor can ignore route updates from a legitimate gateway to deny a node service, trick a legitimate gateway into creating a new, incorrect route so that it is ready to receive redirected traffic, cause traffic forwarded by a gateway to be redirected to a different anchor, or simply have the gateway drop an existing route. Because all mobile node traffic routes through the anchor, a compromised anchor can also intercept, inspect, modify or drop it. The attack can be transient, selectively disabling traffic for a particular node or gateway at particular times, and the anchor can manipulate its routing table so that all packets are directed towards a single gateway, which is a denial of service against that gateway and its access link. The same threats apply to an attacker that tricks a gateway into believing it is the legitimate anchor, which is possible if the two do not mutually authenticate when they establish an association. Such an attacker need not be on the original control plane path, only able to make its presence known to the gateway. An attacker off the data plane path may still be able to intercept traffic by using the protocol to redefine the prefix the node uses in address configuration and pointing that prefix at itself. Whether the node's outgoing packets can then be interfered with depends on the forwarding mechanism: with IP-in-IP encapsulation they can be forced through the attacker, while with standard IP routing they may be relayed via a legitimate anchor and circumvent it.

A compromised gateway can redirect a node's traffic onto its local access link without the node's authorization. This resembles a malicious stub router injecting a bogus host route, but differs in scale: forging a subnet prefix in a link state or distance vector protocol needs the support of several routers, while a bogus host route is likely to take precedence over the routing information advertised by legitimate routers, which is usually less specific, and so the attack should succeed even without support from other routers. Here the damage involves only the compromised gateway and the anchor. A compromised gateway can also ignore a node's presence and refuse to register it, cut the node off by deregistering it as though it had powered down, or trick the anchor into believing that a high number of nodes have attached, so that the anchor creates a routing table entry for each non-existent node until the table's unexpected growth makes it reject legitimate route updates and slows down forwarding. Impersonating a gateway, or replaying route update signaling captured earlier, produces the same effects.

An attacker that interposes itself between a legitimate anchor and a legitimate gateway can act as a man in the middle for both the control plane and the data plane. On the control plane path it can forge, modify or drop route update packets so that incorrect routes are established or routes in active use are removed. On the data plane path it can intercept, inspect, modify, drop and redirect the node's packets. A compromised switch or router between the two causes similar damage and can rewrite IP headers to divert packets from their original path. The attacker can also impersonate the gateway towards the anchor and the other way round, and even when it is off the original data plane path it can have inbound packets routed first to the attacker and then on to the node's gateway and the node itself.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone takes over the anchor or the gateway, they can redirect, drop or read a device's traffic, and can shut other devices off by flooding the anchor with routes for devices that do not exist. Sitting in the middle of the link lets them do the same thing without taking over either end.

sections.title: Threats on the Gateway-to-Device Interface
sections.content:
A gateway watches for the arrival and departure of mobile nodes on its local access link, using link-layer or IP-layer mechanisms. Whatever signaling on the access link is decisive must be securely bound to the mobile node identity, because the gateway uses that binding to ascribe the signaling to the right node and to initiate route update signaling with the anchor. The binding must resist spoofing, or it would let a third party impersonate the node, deny it service, or mount a man-in-the-middle attack.

An attacker able to forge a mobile node's identity can trick the gateway into redirecting the node's packets to the attacker. The attack works against a node on the same link as the attacker, where the redirection happens inside the gateway and involves no route update signaling with the anchor, and against a node on a different link, where the attacker fabricates handoff signaling to make the gateway believe the node has handed over onto its access link. When the attacker and the node connect to different gateways, both gateways think they see the node and both send route updates independently; when they connect to the same gateway, the update is likely to be sent only once and the redirection is internal to it. The node can always recapture its traffic by running handoff signaling again, but standard mobile nodes are generally not prepared to counteract this kind of attack, and even where network stacks include suitable functionality the attack may not be noticeable early enough at the link or IP layer to institute countermeasures quickly. The attack is therefore disruptive at a minimum, and may persist until the node signals again at a subsequent handoff.

Impersonation attacks can be prevented at the link layer, particularly with cellular technologies where the handoff signaling between the mobile node and the network must be authenticated and is completely controlled by the wireless link layer. Cellular access technologies provide a variety of cryptographic and non-cryptographic attack barriers, which makes mounting an impersonation attack, on-link or off-link, very difficult. For non-cellular technologies that do not require link-layer authentication and authorization during handoff, impersonation attacks may be possible. An attacker that can forge handoff signaling can also make the gateway believe a large number of nodes have attached, causing superfluous control plane signaling and needless entries in the gateway's and the anchor's routing tables. An attacker that interposes between the node and the gateway during handoff signaling may be able to mount a man-in-the-middle attack, spoofing the node into believing it has a legitimate connection with the domain, and can then intercept, inspect, modify or drop the node's packets.

A related threat is IP spoofing, used mostly for reflection attacks or to hide the attacker's identity. Wide deployment of network ingress filtering in routers, especially within access networks, contains it, because a router forwards a packet only if the prefix of its IP source address is valid on the router's local access link. An attacker can still use a false interface identifier together with an on-link prefix. In a localized mobility management domain, however, prefixes are not limited to a specific link, so ingress filtering alone becomes insufficient and an additional mechanism for IP address ownership verification is necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The link between the gateway and the device has to be tied to the device's identity, or somebody can pretend to be that device and take its traffic. Cellular links are good at this because they authenticate every handoff. Ordinary Wi-Fi is not, so the memo asks for a separate way to check who owns an address.

sections.title: Flooding Attacks from the Internet
sections.content:
A localized mobility management domain uses an individual host route for the data traffic of each mobile node, between the anchor and the gateway, and creating, maintaining and deleting those routes causes control traffic inside the domain. These characteristics are transparent to mobile nodes and to external correspondent nodes, but they change how much damage a denial-of-service attack from the outside can do.

A denial-of-service attack on an anchor can be launched by sending packets to arbitrary IP addresses that may be in use by mobile nodes in the domain. The anchor sits in a topological position like a border router, through which a substantial amount of data traffic goes, so it must process the flooding packets and perform a routing table lookup for each of them. It can discard packets whose destination address is not registered in its table, but other packets must be encapsulated and forwarded, so a target gateway and the mobile nodes on its access link are likely to suffer as well, because the unrequested packets must be decapsulated and consume link bandwidth and processing capacity on the receivers. The threat is in principle the same as for a denial-of-service attack on a regular IPv6 border router, but because the routing table lookups may let the anchor drop part of the flooding early, or may on the contrary add tunneling workload for packets that cannot be dropped, the impact of an attack against localized mobility management may be different.

In a related attack, the attacker obtains a globally routable IP address of an anchor or of another entity inside the domain and attacks that address. Localized mobility management is in general somewhat resistant to this, because mobile nodes never need a globally routable IP address of any entity in the domain, so a compromised mobile node cannot pass such an address off to a remote attacker, which limits what can be learned about the topology of the domain. It is still possible for an attacker to perform IP address scanning if the gateways and anchors have globally routable addresses, but the much larger IPv6 address space makes scanning considerably more time consuming.
sections.plainLanguage: Flooding a network with traffic aimed at random addresses hurts here in a slightly different way, because the anchor has to look every packet up and tunnel what it cannot drop. The design does help in one respect: devices never need a globally routable address, so they cannot be used to map the network out from outside.

sections.title: Scope and Where the Fixes Live
sections.content: The document describes threats to network-based localized mobility management, and they occur on the two interfaces of the architecture: between the anchor and the gateway, and between the gateway and the mobile node. The mitigation measures, and the security considerations associated with those measures, are described in the protocol specifications for the two interfaces rather than in this memo. The scope is deliberately narrow. The RFC covers only the threats that are peculiar to localized mobility management, and threats to IPv6 in general are documented in RFC 3756.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo names the problems and leaves the repairs to the protocol specifications. It also stays narrow: threats to IPv6 that have nothing to do with mobility are covered elsewhere.

items.text: To one mobile node, or to the whole mobility domain.
